questions.prompt: When writing a unit test for a pure presentational component, what should you primarily verify?

options.text: That the component makes network requests correctly
That the component renders the expected output given its props
That the component's lifecycle methods are called in the right order
That the component's internal state updates as expected

questions.explanation: A pure presentational component's output depends only on its props, so unit tests should assert the rendered UI matches expectations for given prop values.

questions.prompt: In an integration test that checks a form submission flow, why is it common to mock the API call that submits the data?

options.text: To make the test run faster by avoiding real network latency
To ensure the test fails if the backend changes its contract
To prevent the test from accidentally modifying production data
All of the above

questions.explanation: Mocking the API eliminates network variability, isolates the frontend code, and protects against unintended side effects, making integration tests reliable and fast.

questions.prompt: Which testing approach is most appropriate for verifying that a user can navigate from a login page to a dashboard after successful authentication?

options.text: Unit test of the login component's render output
Integration test that mounts the login and dashboard components together
End-to-end test using a browser automation tool
Snapshot test of the login page's DOM

questions.explanation: Verifying a full user navigation flow requires exercising the router, authentication logic, and page transitions, which is best done with an end-to-end test that mimics real user interactions.

questions.prompt: What is a key limitation of snapshot testing for UI components?

options.text: Snapshots cannot capture CSS styles
They provide no insight into which specific element caused a failure
Snapshots only work with functional components
They require a backend server to run

questions.explanation: When a snapshot fails, the diff shows the entire tree change, making it harder to pinpoint the exact element or prop that caused the mismatch without additional inspection.

questions.prompt: Using React Testing Library, which query should you prefer to find a button that has the accessible name 'Submit'?

options.text: getByText(/submit/i)
getByRole('button', { name: /submit/i })
getByTestId('submit-button')
getByLabelText('Submit')

questions.explanation: getByRole with a name argument respects accessibility semantics and finds elements by their accessible name, which is the recommended way to query interactive components.

questions.prompt: Why is the act() utility necessary when testing asynchronous state updates in React components?

options.text: To ensure React flushes all pending updates before making assertions
To prevent the test runner from timing out
To mock the component's props during render
To convert synchronous code into asynchronous code

questions.explanation: act() wraps the code that triggers updates, guaranteeing that React processes all state changes and effects before the test runs its expectations, avoiding warnings about unflushed updates.
